questions.q: Name FOUR distinct application domains of gene cloning and give ONE specific product/example for each domain that is commercially used in India.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Medical — recombinant human insulin (Humulin) produced in E. coli; (2) Agricultural — Bt cotton (Cry1Ac gene from Bacillus thuringiensis) for bollworm resistance; (3) Industrial — recombinant rennet (chymosin) for cheese production replacing calf stomach extract; (4) Research/Forensic — DNA fingerprinting kits using VNTR/STR probes for paternity testing and crime investigation. A wrong answer revealing misconception: listing "PCR" as an application domain instead of a technique used across domains, or citing "Golden Rice" as currently commercialized in India (it is approved but not yet widely cultivated).

questions.q: Explain why human insulin produced in E. coli via gene cloning is therapeutically superior to porcine insulin extracted from pig pancreases, addressing at least THREE factors: immunogenicity, supply scalability, and batch consistency.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Immunogenicity: Human insulin differs from porcine insulin by one amino acid (Thr vs Ala at B30); cloned human insulin is identical to native human insulin, eliminating anti-insulin antibody formation. (2) Supply scalability: Fermentation of recombinant E. coli yields grams of insulin per litre, unlimited by pancreas availability; porcine insulin requires ~50,000 pig pancreases per kg of insulin. (3) Batch consistency: Cloned gene ensures identical amino acid sequence every batch; porcine extraction varies with animal age, diet, and processing. Wrong answer reveals: confusing "porcine insulin is identical to human" (it is not), or thinking scalability is limited by plasmid copy number (industrial strains use high-copy vectors and optimized fermentation).

questions.q: A biotech startup wants to produce a human glycoprotein therapeutic (e.g., erythropoietin) that requires N-linked glycosylation for activity. They have the cDNA clone. Should they use E. coli or a mammalian cell line (CHO cells) as host? Justify your choice with TWO specific molecular reasons.
questions.a: Correct answer: Choose CHO cells (Chinese Hamster Ovary). Reason 1: E. coli lacks the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus required for N-linked glycosylation; it cannot attach complex oligosaccharides to Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequons. Reason 2: E. coli lacks chaperones (e.g., BiP, calnexin) for proper folding of complex eukaryotic glycoproteins, leading to inclusion bodies. Wrong answer reveals: choosing E. coli because "it grows faster and gives higher yield" ignoring that the product would be inactive aglycosylated protein; or suggesting yeast (Pichia) without noting its hyperglycosylation (α-1,3-mannose) causes immunogenicity in humans.

questions.q: Compare the cloning strategy for producing Bt toxin (Cry protein) in cotton plants versus producing the same toxin in E. coli for biopesticide spray formulation. Analyze FOUR differences: (a) vector type, (b) promoter choice, (c) selection marker, (d) downstream processing.
questions.a: Correct answer: (a) Vector: Cotton uses Agrobacterium Ti-plasmid derived binary vector (T-DNA borders); E. coli uses high-copy plasmid (pBR322/pUC origin). (b) Promoter: Cotton needs constitutive plant promoter (CaMV 35S) or tissue-specific (e.g., Cry1Ac under green tissue promoter); E. coli uses strong inducible promoter (T7/lac, tac) for controlled expression. (c) Selection: Cotton uses nptII (kanamycin) or bar (phosphinothricin) for plant cell selection; E. coli uses ampR (ampicillin) for bacterial selection. (d) Downstream: Cotton expresses toxin in planta — no purification needed; E. coli requires fermentation, cell lysis, inclusion body solubilization, refolding, and purification for spray formulation. Wrong answer reveals: using same promoter (e.g., T7) for both hosts (T7 requires T7 RNAP absent in plants), or ignoring that plant-expressed Cry protein must be stable in chloroplasts/cytoplasm while bacterial expression often forms inclusion bodies needing refolding.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "RT-PCR based COVID-19 diagnostic kits are a direct application of gene cloning technology." Support or refute with THREE specific technical connections linking cloning steps (cDNA synthesis, amplification, probe design) to the RT-PCR workflow.
questions.a: Correct answer: SUPPORT the claim. Three connections: (1) cDNA synthesis: RT-PCR uses reverse transcriptase (studied in c12_biotech_cbse_03_003) to convert viral RNA to cDNA — identical to cDNA library construction. (2) Amplification: PCR uses Taq polymerase (c12_biotech_cbse_03_007) to amplify specific viral gene regions (ORF1ab, N, S genes) — same principle as amplifying cloned inserts. (3) Probe design: TaqMan probes are synthetic oligonucleotides complementary to target sequences — designed using known viral genome sequences obtained via cloning and sequencing (c12_biotech_cbse_03_008, 03_009). Refutation reveals: thinking RT-PCR "clones the virus" (it amplifies, does not clone into vectors), or missing that probe specificity relies on prior cloning/sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 genome.

questions.q: Design a gene cloning workflow to produce a thermostable α-amylase for the Indian textile industry (desizing cotton fabric at 80°C). Specify: (a) gene source organism, (b) vector and host system, (c) selection/screening method, (d) one industrial scale-up consideration. Justify each choice.
questions.a: Expected answer: (a) Gene source: Thermophilic bacterium (e.g., Bacillus licheniformis, Geobacillus stearothermophilus) or archaea (Pyrococcus furiosus) — naturally thermostable α-amylase genes. (b) Vector/host: Expression vector (pET series) in E. coli BL21(DE3) for high-level T7-driven expression; alternatively Bacillus subtilis secretion system for extracellular production. (c) Screening: Activity-based screening on starch-agar plates at 70°C (iodine staining shows clearance zones) OR SDS-PAGE of induced lysates with activity assay. (d) Scale-up: Fed-batch fermentation with controlled glucose feeding to avoid acetate accumulation; downstream: cell lysis, heat treatment (70°C, 30 min) to denature host proteins while thermostable amylase remains active — simplifies purification. Poor answer reveals: using mesophilic amylase gene (e.g., from E. coli) ignoring thermostability requirement; choosing constitutive promoter causing toxicity; omitting heat-stable purification step that exploits the enzyme's property.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ of gene cloning refer to the practical utilization of recombinant DNA technology to produce valuable proteins, engineer organisms with desired traits, diagnose diseases, and advance scientific research across medicine, agriculture, industry, and forensics by leveraging cloned genes and their expression products.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a diabetic patient in India who needs insulin daily — historically extracted from pig ______ with limited supply and allergic reactions.
Fill in the blank: We then extend this logic to Bt cotton, COVID-______ RT-PCR kits, and industrial enzymes — showing how the SAME cloning toolkit solves diverse problems.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) categorize a given real-world biotechnology product or technique into medical, agricultural, industrial, or research application domains with justification, and (2) design a logical cloning strategy (vector choice, host, selection method) for a specified application scenario such as producing human.
